headline: Russia Sanctions Pause Deepens Ukraine Rift
dek: Fighting spread from Ukraine’s energy grid to Black Sea shipping while Houthi attacks widened, public institutions faced pressure, and school communities absorbed fresh losses.

segments.text: Happy Saturday, the week’s clearest change was not a new peace process but the further erosion of one: a claimed energy ceasefire in Ukraine gave way to continued strikes, renewed attacks on Russian energy targets, and a U.S. pause in new Russia sanctions. At the same time, Houthi attacks expanded the regional conflict’s reach, and emergencies in Oregon and Pakistan put the consequences of institutional failures in painfully local terms. The connective thread was the fragility of protections—diplomatic, civic, and physical—when events move faster than the systems meant to contain them.

sections.title: Ukraine diplomacy gives way to escalation
sections.kicker: A ceasefire claim did not hold on the ground

segments.text: The week began with President Donald Trump announcing a diesel arrangement with Russia and then saying that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to an “energy ceasefire.” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly questioned whether such an agreement existed, and Ukrainian officials reported Russian strikes on energy facilities soon afterward. By midweek, Russian attacks had again damaged homes, factories and power infrastructure in several Ukrainian cities, while Kyiv said restrictions on Starlink access were compounding operational pressure. The practical result was a widening gap between diplomatic declarations and the war’s daily reality.

Ukraine responded by ending its pause on attacks against Russian refineries, saying Russia had never stopped targeting Ukrainian infrastructure. On Friday, Trump put recently enacted Russia sanctions on hold, citing the national interest; Zelenskyy argued that the decision would reward Moscow. The fighting also carried risks beyond Ukraine’s borders: suspected drone strikes against commercial shipping in the Black Sea left people dead or missing and raised concern about a vital shipping route. This is now more than a dispute over a failed truce. It is a test of whether external leverage can restrain a war when both sides see energy systems as military targets.

sections.title: Houthi attacks widen a regional conflict
sections.kicker: Airports, oil infrastructure and Yemen’s government came under pressure

segments.text: The conflict involving Saudi Arabia, the Houthis and Iran-aligned forces continued to expand in scope. Repeated Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed at least 13 people and injured hundreds, according to reporting during the week, forcing an extended suspension of flights. Saudi officials also examined how their defenses failed to stop the attacks, while the coalition reported intercepting another missile aimed at Riyadh. What had begun with strikes on airport facilities became a sustained challenge to civilian aviation, air defense and public confidence in the kingdom’s security infrastructure.

The geographic range widened further. Houthi forces struck the presidential palace in Aden, seat of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, causing reported casualties; by Friday, Aden airport had also been hit by missiles for the second time in less than two weeks. Iran denied Saudi accusations that it had encouraged or directed the escalation. The denial matters because attribution remains central to the risk of a wider confrontation: Saudi and U.S. officials have treated Houthi operations as part of a broader Iranian challenge, while Tehran rejects responsibility. For civilians, however, the immediate pattern is clearer—transport hubs and government sites are increasingly exposed.

sections.title: Public scrutiny faces renewed pressure
sections.kicker: Courts, protests and newsrooms became arenas of accountability

segments.text: In Washington, a federal judge kept in place protections allowing CNN, MS NOW and Politico to retain White House access while their challenge to the administration’s restrictions proceeds. The ruling came after the Justice Department had investigated major television networks over their temporary suspension of press-pool coverage—a striking escalation in a dispute over how the presidency is covered. The week also brought a quick personnel drama: Katie Zacharia, appointed as White House press secretary, faced questions about her claimed legal credentials and left the role after five days. The episodes were different in scale, but both concerned the credibility and independence of public-facing institutions.

Elsewhere, the struggle over who may question authority was more direct. In Delhi, police again detained Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the “Cockroach” movement, before a planned protest over contested voter-list revisions; he was released the following day under conditions. In Istanbul, Turkish authorities raided Halk TV, halted broadcasts and appointed a trustee to run the independent channel, prompting condemnation from opposition figures and rights groups. These cases should not be collapsed into one story. Yet together they show why procedures such as press access, protest rights and legal review matter: they are the mechanisms through which claims of official power can be tested in public.

sections.title: Two school tragedies, different failures
sections.kicker: Communities in Oregon and Pakistan seek answers

segments.text: At Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, three children and a teacher were killed when a former student opened fire with a shotgun. Police said the 16-year-old fired about 15 rounds before he was stopped and killed after intervention by a teacher and community members. Two people were critically injured. A candlelight vigil followed as the community learned more about the victims and the attempts to interrupt the attack. The investigation will inevitably examine access to the weapon and the sequence of the response, but the immediate fact is a familiar and devastating one: an elementary school became the site of sudden, irreversible loss.

In Peshawar, Pakistan, at least 35 people—including 34 children and a teacher—were killed when the roof of a private school collapsed. More than 50 others were reported injured. Authorities arrested the school owner and ordered inspections of school infrastructure after families said warnings had been raised about the building’s condition; early reporting pointed to weak construction and work that may have overloaded the roof. The Oregon and Peshawar deaths came from profoundly different circumstances, so they demand different answers. But both place responsibility on adults and institutions whose essential duty is to make learning spaces safe before a crisis begins.
